section: Abstract
claim_text: **Results:** Day-2 energy was 105–166 kcal below day-1 energy in 2011–2018, with no heterogeneity detected on the log scale (P = 0.77), but 34 kcal higher in 2021–2023. The estimated first-recall reporting reduction was 9.1% (95% CI: 7.2, 11.0). In complete cases, reported energy was 130 kcal/d (77, 184) below the 2017–2018 mean; after correction, it was 73 kcal/d (6, 141) above it. The beverage, snack, sweet, and addition pool accounted for 68.7% (50.0, 87.5) of the kcal shift versus 34.5% of baseline energy under the control mean, and 49.1% (21.8, 76.3) under the trend reference. The item-count component failed the pre-trend criterion, making its decomposition conditional. Total sugars met the criterion and were reported 10.5% (6.6, 14.2) lower under the control mean.

section: Introduction
claim_text: NHANES changed the first-recall protocol in August 2021–August 2023. Telephone administration replaced the MEC interview, a take-home food-model booklet replaced the examination center’s portion models, and the interview moved to 3–7 days after the examination; the second telephone recall followed 3–10 days later (3, 4, 5). The change was not piloted (3). An NCHS white paper described lower day-1 energy and a reversal in the day-1 minus day-2 difference in foods reported, but it did not separate the reporting effect from secular change with statistical inference, identify which foods accounted for it, or quantify its consequences for population estimates (3). Federal reports have since used these day-1 data in trends spanning the change (6, 7).

section: Food-level decomposition
claim_text: Among adults with positive energy (E) and item counts (N) on both days, log E = log N + log(E/N) exactly, so the DiD in log E equals the sum of the DiDs in log N and in log energy per item; we report the item-count share, DiD(log N)/DiD(log E). We also partitioned kcal and item counts additively by eating occasion (meals, snacks and drinks, other) and food group. For each kcal component g, the overrepresentation ratio R_g was its share of the total kcal DiD divided by its share of control-period day-1 energy. Before outcome estimation, we specified a pooled group of non-alcoholic beverages, alcoholic beverages, snacks and sweets, and additions (fats, condiments, and sugars); a pooled R interval above one indicated disproportionate representation. Individual R_g were tested against one using bootstrap SEs and t with 77 df, with BH correction within occasions and within food groups under each reference. A control-mean q < 0.05 also required the trend-reference R_g − 1 to share its sign. Grams per item, including analyses restricted to two-day consumers of a group, were descriptive. Component pre-trends used the primary criterion (Tables S10–S12). The extension reused the original covariates, references, and bootstrap multipliers (Supplementary Methods).

For each kcal component g, the overrepresentation ratio R_g was its share of the total kcal DiD divided by its share of control-period day-1 energy. Individual R_g were tested against one using bootstrap SEs and t with 77 df, with BH correction within occasions and within food groups under each reference. A control-mean q < 0.05 also required the trend-reference R_g − 1 to share its sign. Grams per item, including analyses restricted to two-day consumers of a group, were descriptive. Component pre-trends used the primary criterion (Tables S10–S12). The extension reused the original covariates, references, and bootstrap multipliers (Supplementary Methods).

section: Consequences for population means and trends
claim_text: Correction raised the 2021–2023 first-recall energy mean from 2,026 kcal/d (95% CI: 1,992, 2,060) to 2,229 (2,178, 2,280), a difference of 203 kcal/d (158, 248) under the control-mean reference and 209 (110, 307) under the trend reference (Figure 3; Table 2). In complete cases, reported 2021–2023 energy was 130 kcal/d (77, 184) below the 2017–2018 mean. After correction, it was 73 kcal/d (6, 141) above that mean under the control-mean reference and 79 (−33, 190) above it under the trend reference (Table S13). Under the stable-order-effect assumption, the observed decline therefore did not persist on the earlier reporting scale. Second-recall energy, collected by telephone in both periods, was 0.040 log units (0.002, 0.077) higher in 2021–2023 than in 2017–2018 (Table S4).

section: Discussion
claim_text: The pattern is compatible with how the multiple-pass method retrieves foods. Its forgotten-foods pass probes specifically for beverages, sweets, and snacks, which respondents often leave out of their first listing (2). Before 2021, this probing took place face to face at the MEC, with three-dimensional portion models. In 2021–2023, it took place by telephone, with a take-home booklet. The control-mean contrasts in energy per item and grams per item are compatible with changes in the mix of reported items. Grams per item were descriptive, did not meet the pre-trend criterion, and depended on the reference, so they do not establish which foods or portions changed. These analyses do not establish omission of specific foods, and item counts also depend on how foods and additions are coded. The simultaneous changes in mode, portion aids, and timing cannot be separated. Earlier controlled comparisons found broadly similar performance of telephone and in-person multiple-pass recalls (15–17), but these studies do not identify the separate effects of the present survey changes. A non-peer-reviewed analysis reported changes in beverage-dominated components consistent with ours (18).

section: Discussion
claim_text: These findings motivate outcome-specific checks for surveillance and exposure assessment involving beverages and discretionary foods (1, 18). They do not establish effects for individual beverages or added sugars, and caffeine did not meet the pre-trend criterion. Three practices follow for users of NHANES dietary data. First, analyses spanning 2021–2023 should address the reporting-scale break outcome by outcome rather than assume that energy-adjusted measures are protected. For fast-food energy percentage, we reproduced the published decline from 14.1% to 11.7%, but the pre-trend criterion was not met and a correction is not identified (Table S8). Second, usual-intake models should allow the first-recall effect in this cycle to differ from that in earlier cycles. Third, comparisons of intake distributions and inadequacy prevalence should use a common reporting scale; the illustrative calcium calculation indicates the potential magnitude. We draw no conclusion about iron inadequacy.

claim_text: We used ncimultivar 1.1.2 to fit the NCI multivariate daily-amount model jointly to iron and calcium, using the package’s weighted Box–Cox transformation procedure. The models included both reliable recalls, two-day dietary weights, the fixed covariates, and a recall-order indicator. Correction was exp[log(intake + 1) + DiD] − 1; the second-recall vector remained unchanged. The full-sample models used four chains of 12,000 iterations, burn-in of 2,000, and thinning by 25; the maximum R̂ was 1.006.

claim_text: The combined design contained 74 strata and 151 PSUs. claim_text: Replicate models used four chains of 3,000 iterations, burn-in of 1,000, and thinning by 5.
